In this exercise we will model lake ice duration data using linear regression models. According to the United States Environmental Protection Agency, lake ice duration can be an indicator of climate change. This is because lake ice is dependent on several environmental factors, so changes in these factors will influence the formation of ice on top of lakes. As a result, the study and analysis of lake ice formation can inform scientists about how quickly the climate is changing, and are critical to minimizing disruptions to lake ecosystems. We can examine the ice duration of Lake Mendota and Lake Monona in the are of Madison, WI. The dataset is extracted from the `ntl_icecover` dataset of the `R` package `lterdatasampler`.

::: {style="text-align:center;"}


```{R, out.width = "100%", echo = F}
knitr::include_graphics("../class4/img/lakeice.jpg")
```

:::


You can load the data as follows:
```{python, echo=TRUE}

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
df_icecover = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ELSTE-Master/Data-Science/main/Data/df_icecover.csv")
df_icecover.head()
```

plt.xticks(rotation=45)
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()

### Question 2
One of your colleague proposes to consider the following models to analyze the ice duration data:
$$
\text{IceCover}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Year}_i + \epsilon_i
$$
He estimates the model and obtain the following results:
```{python, echo=TRUE}
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import numpy as np

df_icecover = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ELSTE-Master/Data-Science/main/Data/df_icecover.csv")
mod1 = smf.ols("ice_duration ~ year", data=df_icecover).fit()
print(mod1.summary())
```

He wants to test if the ice duration is reducing over the years, regardless of the lake. What are the correct hyptheses to test this claim?

```{r, results='asis'}
# Define questions choice and individual feedback for each question
opts <- list(
  answer = list(
    value = "\\( H_0: \\beta_1 = 0 \\), \\( H_a: \\beta_1 < 0 \\)",
    feedback = "Yes! The alternative hypothesis tests if ice duration decreases over the years."
  ),
  list(
    value = "\\( H_0: \\beta_1 = 0 \\), \\( H_a: \\beta_1 > 0 \\)",
    feedback = "No, this would test if ice duration is increasing over the years."
  ),
  list(
    value = "\\( H_0: \\beta_1 = 0 \\), \\( H_a: \\beta_1 \\neq 0 \\)",
    feedback = "This tests for any change (increase or decrease), not specifically a reduction."
  ),
  list(
    value = "\\( H_0: \\beta_1 \\neq 0 \\), \\( H_a: \\beta_1 = 0 \\)",
    feedback = "No, the null hypothesis should always contain equality."
  )
)
# render QA environment
render_q_a_env(opts)
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_2
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import numpy as np

# Load data
df_icecover = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ELSTE-Master/Data-Science/main/Data/df_icecover.csv")

# Fit linear model with lake-specific intercepts
mod2 = smf.ols("ice_duration ~ year + lakeid", data=df_icecover).fit()
print(mod2.summary())

# Separate lakes
df_mendota = df_icecover[df_icecover['lakeid'] == "Lake Mendota"]
df_monona  = df_icecover[df_icecover['lakeid'] == "Lake Monona"]

# Colors
colors = ["#6a5acd", "#e64173"]

# Plot data points
plt.figure(figsize=(8,5))
plt.scatter(df_mendota['year'], df_mendota['ice_duration'], color=colors[0], label="Mendota")
plt.scatter(df_monona['year'], df_monona['ice_duration'], color=colors[1], label="Monona")

# Prepare years for predictions
years = np.linspace(df_icecover['year'].min(), df_icecover['year'].max(), 200)

# Predict for Mendota
pred_mendota = mod2.______(pd.DataFrame({'year': years, 'lakeid': 'Lake Mendota'}))
plt.plot(years, pred_mendota, color=colors[0], linestyle='-', linewidth=2)

# Predict for Monona
pred_monona = mod2.______(pd.DataFrame({'year': years, 'lakeid': 'Lake Monona'}))
plt.plot(years, pred_monona, color=colors[1], linestyle='-', linewidth=2)

# Labels, legend, title
plt.xlabel("Year")
plt.ylabel("Ice duration (days)")
plt.title("Ice duration over years with regression lines")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()

```

## Solution

::: { .solution exercise="ex_2" }

```python
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import numpy as np

# Load data
df_icecover = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ELSTE-Master/Data-Science/main/Data/df_icecover.csv")

# Fit linear model with lake-specific intercepts
mod2 = smf.ols("ice_duration ~ year + lakeid", data=df_icecover).fit()
print(mod2.summary())

# Separate lakes
df_mendota = df_icecover[df_icecover['lakeid'] == "Lake Mendota"]
df_monona  = df_icecover[df_icecover['lakeid'] == "Lake Monona"]

# Colors
colors = ["#6a5acd", "#e64173"]

# Plot data points
plt.figure(figsize=(8,5))
plt.scatter(df_mendota['year'], df_mendota['ice_duration'], color=colors[0], label="Mendota")
plt.scatter(df_monona['year'], df_monona['ice_duration'], color=colors[1], label="Monona")

# Prepare years for predictions
years = np.linspace(df_icecover['year'].min(), df_icecover['year'].max(), 200)

# Predict for Mendota
pred_mendota = mod2.predict(pd.DataFrame({'year': years, 'lakeid': 'Lake Mendota'}))
plt.plot(years, pred_mendota, color=colors[0], linestyle='-', linewidth=2)

# Predict for Monona
pred_monona = mod2.predict(pd.DataFrame({'year': years, 'lakeid': 'Lake Monona'}))
plt.plot(years, pred_monona, color=colors[1], linestyle='-', linewidth=2)

# Labels, legend, title
plt.xlabel("Year")
plt.ylabel("Ice duration (days)")
plt.title("Ice duration over years with regression lines")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()

```

### Question 5
A third colleague of yours proposes to consider the following model to analyze the ice duration data:
$$
\text{IceCover}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Year}_i + \beta_2 \text{LakeID}_i + \beta_3 \text{Year}_i \times \text{LakeID}_i + \epsilon_i
$$
What is the correct formula to specify this model in `statsmodels`?

```{r, results='asis'}
# Define questions choice and individual feedback for each question
opts <- list(
 
  list(
    value = "<code>ice_duration ~ year + lakeid</code>",
    feedback = "No, this formula does not include the interaction term."
  ),
  list(
    value = "<code>ice_duration ~ year</code>",
    feedback = "No, this formula does not include lakeid or the interaction term."
  ),
   answer = list(
    value = "<code>ice_duration ~ year * lakeid</code>",
    feedback = "Correct! The <code>*</code> operator includes both main effects and the interaction term."
  ),
  list(
    value = "<code>ice_duration ~ year / lakeid</code>",
    feedback = "No, the <code>/</code> operator is not used for interactions in `statsmodels`."
  )
)
# render QA environment
render_q_a_env(opts)
```

```python
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import numpy as np

# Load data
df_icecover = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ELSTE-Master/Data-Science/main/Data/df_icecover.csv")

# Fit linear model with lake-specific intercepts
mod3 = smf.ols("ice_duration ~ year + lakeid + year:lakeid", data=df_icecover).fit()
print(mod3.summary())

# Separate lakes
df_mendota = df_icecover[df_icecover['lakeid'] == "Lake Mendota"]
df_monona  = df_icecover[df_icecover['lakeid'] == "Lake Monona"]

# Colors
colors = ["#6a5acd", "#e64173"]

# Plot data points
plt.figure(figsize=(8,5))
plt.scatter(df_mendota['year'], df_mendota['ice_duration'], color=colors[0], label="Mendota")
plt.scatter(df_monona['year'], df_monona['ice_duration'], color=colors[1], label="Monona")

# Prepare years for predictions
years = np.linspace(df_icecover['year'].min(), df_icecover['year'].max(), 200)

# Predict for Mendota
pred_mendota = mod3.predict(pd.DataFrame({'year': years, 'lakeid': 'Lake Mendota'}))
plt.plot(years, pred_mendota, color=colors[0], linestyle='-', linewidth=2)

# Predict for Monona
pred_monona = mod3.predict(pd.DataFrame({'year': years, 'lakeid': 'Lake Monona'}))
plt.plot(years, pred_monona, color=colors[1], linestyle='-', linewidth=2)

# Labels, legend, title
plt.xlabel("Year")
plt.ylabel("Ice duration (days)")
plt.title("Ice duration over years with regression lines")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()

```

### Question 10

A climatologist uses `mod3` to predict the ice duration in the year $2500$ for both lakes and obtains the following results:

```{python, echo=TRUE}
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import numpy as np

# Load data
df_icecover = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ELSTE-Master/Data-Science/main/Data/df_icecover.csv")
# Fit linear model with lake-specific intercepts and trend
mod3 = smf.ols("ice_duration ~ year + lakeid + year:lakeid", data=df_icecover).fit()
# Define levels for the categorical variable
lake_levels = df_icecover['lakeid'].astype('category').cat.categories
# Predict for Mendota
pred_mendota = mod3.predict(pd.DataFrame({
    'year': [2500], 
    'lakeid': pd.Categorical(['Lake Mendota'], categories=lake_levels)
}))
# Predict for Monona
pred_monona = mod3.predict(pd.DataFrame({
    'year': [2500], 
    'lakeid': pd.Categorical(['Lake Monona'], categories=lake_levels)
}))

print(f"Predicted ice duration in 2500 for Lake Mendota: {pred_mendota.values[0]:.2f} days")
print(f"Predicted ice duration in 2500 for Lake Monona: {pred_monona.values[0]:.2f} days")
```
Is this prediction reliable? Justify your answer.




```{r, results='asis'}
# Define questions choice and individual feedback for each question

  ),
  answer = list(
    value = "No. The prediction is not reliable. It is a large extrapolation beyond the data range and even yields an impossible/negative ice duration.",
    feedback = "Correct! Predicting for year \\(2500\\) is extreme extrapolation. Linear model behavior outside the observed years is uncertain."
  ),
  list(
    value = "No. Because the interaction term is not statistically significant, the model cannot be used for prediction at all.",
    feedback = "No. Non-significant interaction only means there is little evidence of different slopes between lakes in the sample. The main issue here is extrapolation and unrealistic predicted values."
  ),
  list(
    value = "Yes, predictions at any year are valid.",
    feedback = "No."
  )
)

# render QA environment
render_q_a_env(opts)
```






### Question 11
Based on the AIC values, which model would you select among the three models fitted above?

```{python, echo=TRUE}
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import numpy as np
df_icecover = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ELSTE-Master/Data-Science/main/Data/df_icecover.csv")
mod1 = smf.ols("ice_duration ~ year", data=df_icecover).fit()
mod2 = smf.ols("ice_duration ~ year + lakeid", data=df_icecover).fit()
mod3 = smf.ols("ice_duration ~ year + lakeid + year:lakeid", data=df_icecover).fit()
aic_values = pd.DataFrame({
    'Model': ['mod1', 'mod2', 'mod3'],
    'AIC': [mod1.aic, mod2.aic, mod3.aic]
})
print(aic_values)
```


```{r, results='asis'}
opts <- list(
  list(
    value = "Model 3, because it is the most complex and therefore should always fit the data best.",
    feedback = "No. Although more complex models can fit data better, AIC penalizes complexity. Model 3 has the highest AIC, so it is not preferred."
  ),
  
  list(
    value = "Model 2 (with lake-specific intercepts), because it has the lowest AIC among the three models.",
    feedback = "No. Model 2’s AIC (2819.40) is higher than Model 1’s (2817.76), so Model 1 is preferred."
  ),
  answer = list(
    value = "Model 1, because it has the lowest AIC among the three models.",
    feedback = "Correct! Model 1 has the smallest AIC value (2817.76), indicating it provides the best balance between model fit and simplicity."
  ),
  list(
    value = "Model 1, because simpler models are always better regardless of AIC.",
    feedback = "Not quite. Model 1 is preferred because it actually has the lowest AIC, not just because it’s simpler."
  )
)


# render QA environment
render_q_a_env(opts)
```








### Question 12
An expert says that the data are actually not independent because the ice duration in a given year might be correlated with the ice duration in the previous year. Is this a problem to perform inference with the models fitted above?



```{r, results='asis'}
opts <- list(
  list(
    value = "No, correlation between observations across years does not matter for linear regression.",
    feedback = "No. Autocorrelation violates the independence assumption of the residuals, which can make standard errors and hypothesis tests unreliable."
  ),
  answer = list(
    value = "Yes, it can be a problem because correlated observations violate the independence assumption required for linear regression.",
    feedback = "Correct! When residuals are autocorrelated, standard errors may be underestimated, leading to incorrect p-values and confidence intervals."
  ),
  list(
    value = "No, as long as the model includes <code>year</code> as a covariate, independence is automatically ensured.",
    feedback = "No. Including 'year' as a covariate does not guarantee that residuals are independent across time."
  ),
  list(
    value = "Yes, but only if the sample size is very small.",
    feedback = "Autocorrelation affects inference regardless of sample size."
  )
)

# render QA environment
render_q_a_env(opts)

```
